## Source versions

Earliest listed publication among matched versions, not proof of an unedited contemporaneous archive. Claim timestamps refer to the reviewed version.

## Summary

Eisman separates war-driven inflation risk from AI capital returns and private-credit stress. He distinguishes retail fund liquidity from underlying credit quality, but overstates the absence of prior credit cycles and treats SoFi securitization access as indispensable despite its deposit-funded bank. Software refinancing and related-party asset transfers are material concerns whose magnitude remains unresolved. He endorses transparency and incentive reform in drug pricing without endorsing price controls.

Full transcript read. This bounded evidence audit retains unresolved outcomes where matched primary verification is missing; those are not adverse accuracy grades.

## Framework and tools

- Separate liquidity constraints from realized credit losses.
- Follow fast credit growth and sector concentrations.
- Stress the financing waterfall rather than just headline asset value.
- Distinguish AI supplier spending from eventual investor returns.
- Demand transparency in both credit marks and healthcare incentives.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- 10-year Treasury yield versus oil
- Fertilizer price index
- Private-credit market growth and software exposure
- Quarterly redemption caps versus requests
- Securitization cumulative-net-loss triggers and waterfalls
- PBM rebates and Cost Plus markup

## Source cautions

Steve Eisman is the sole substantive speaker; viewer questions are distinguished from his responses.
- Recorded March 19, published March 20.
- Opening montage repeats later statements and is not separately counted.
- Caption names Treasury Secretary Mnuchin; contemporary identity needs checking before attribution.
- MFS is called MFS Investment Management here, whereas the March 6 episode identifies Market Financial Solutions; do not transfer fraud allegations to the unrelated asset manager.
- SoFi illustrative 10%/5% rates are annualized yields, despite monthly wording.
- Viewer drug-pricing argument is a question, not automatically Eisman endorsement.
